**Structure:** Three books in sixty numbered parts. ## Author's thesis (paraphrased from source)

The *Rhetoric* opens: *"Rhetoric is the counterpart of Dialectic."* [V] (Bk I, Part 1) Both deal with matters that come, more or less, within the general ken of all men and belong to no definite science, and both draw opposite conclusions impartially. Rhetoric is defined as *"the faculty of observing in any given case the available means of persuasion"* [V] (Bk I, Part 2), and its function is *"not simply to succeed in persuading, but rather to discover the means of coming as near such success as the circumstances of each particular case allow"* [V] (Bk I, Part 1), on the analogy of medicine, which puts a patient as far as may be on the road to health. [AR]

The art's substance is proof. The author charges the writers of current treatises with saying *"nothing about enthymemes, which are the substance of rhetorical persuasion"* [V] and with dealing *"mainly with non-essentials"* [V] such as arousing prejudice, pity and anger (Bk I, Part 1). Yet he names three modes of persuasion furnished by the spoken word: *"The first kind depends on the personal character of the speaker; the second on putting the audience into a certain frame of mind; the third on the proof, or apparent proof, provided by the words of the speech itself."* [V] (Bk I, Part 2) The person who commands them must be able to reason logically, to understand character and goodness, and to understand the emotions, so rhetoric is *"an offshoot of dialectic and also of ethical studies"* [V] (Bk I, Part 2). Book II gives the reason for treating character and emotion at length: because *"rhetoric exists to affect the giving of decisions"* [V], the orator *"must also make his own character look right and put his hearers, who are to decide, into the right frame of mind"* [V] (Bk II, Part 1). Book III adds that attention to delivery and style is needed *"owing to the defects of our hearers"* [V], while *"we ought in fairness to fight our case with no help beyond the bare facts"* [V] (Bk III, Part 1). [AR]

The hearer sets the divisions of the art. Of speaker, subject and person addressed, *"it is the last one, the hearer, that determines the speech's end and object"* [V] (Bk I, Part 3). Hearers who decide about the future make political oratory, aimed at the expedient or harmful; hearers who decide about the past make forensic oratory, aimed at the just or unjust; hearers who judge the speaker's skill make ceremonial oratory, aimed at the honourable or dishonourable (Bk I, Part 3). Rhetoric deals with *"such matters as we deliberate upon without arts or systems to guide us, in the hearing of persons who cannot take in at a glance a complicated argument, or follow a long chain of reasoning"* [V] (Bk I, Part 2), so the enthymeme is a compressed syllogism from probabilities and signs, and the example a rhetorical induction. Book II, Part 18 restates the frame: *"The use of persuasive speech is to lead to decisions."* [V] (Bk II, Part 18) [AR]

The work's order follows the author's three points of a speech: the means of persuasion (Books I and II), style and arrangement (Book III). Throughout, the author treats rhetoric as able to argue either side, but holds that the speaker *"must not make people believe what is wrong"* [V] and that *"things that are true and things that are better are, by their nature, practically always easier to prove and easier to believe in"* [V] (Bk I, Part 1). [AR]

## Theme 1: What rhetoric is (Bk I, Parts 1–3)

### Bk I, Part 1: the counterpart of dialectic

All men use rhetoric and dialectic more or less, at random or from habit; since some succeed through practice and others spontaneously, the subject can be handled systematically, and *"every one will at once agree that such an inquiry is the function of an art"* [V] (Bk I, Part 1). *"The modes of persuasion are the only true constituents of the art: everything else is merely accessory."* [V] (Bk I, Part 1) [AR]

The current treatises, the author says, deal with non-essentials: the arousing of prejudice, pity and anger *"has nothing to do with the essential facts, but is merely a personal appeal to the man who is judging the case"* [V]. *"It is not right to pervert the judge by moving him to anger or envy or pity-one might as well warp a carpenter's rule before using it."* [V] (Bk I, Part 1) He approves the court of Areopagus, which forbids talk about non-essentials, as *"sound law and custom"* [V]. [AR]

Well-drawn laws should define as much as possible and leave as little as possible to judges, for three reasons: a few sensible lawgivers are easier to find than many; laws are made after long consideration while court decisions come at short notice; and *"the decision of the lawgiver is not particular but prospective and general"* [V], whereas assembly members and jurors decide definite cases and are swayed by *"feelings of friendship or hatred or self-interest"* [V] (Bk I, Part 1). Questions of whether something happened must still be left to the judge. Writers who lay down rules for the contents of the "introduction" or "narration" are *"theorizing about non-essentials as if they belonged to the art"* [V]. [AR]

The same principles apply to political and forensic oratory, and political oratory is *"a nobler business, and fitter for a citizen"* [V], but the treatise-writers neglect it because it gives less inducement to talk about non-essentials: in a political debate the man judging *"is making a decision about his own vital interests"* [V], while in forensic oratory it is other people's affairs that are decided, and *"to conciliate the listener is what pays here"* [V] (Bk I, Part 1). [AR]

Rhetorical study in its strict sense concerns the modes of persuasion; persuasion is *"a sort of demonstration"* [V]; the orator's demonstration is the enthymeme, a sort of syllogism, so the person best able to see how and from what elements a syllogism is produced will be best skilled in enthymemes once he has also learnt their subject-matter and how they differ from syllogisms of strict logic. *"The true and the approximately true are apprehended by the same faculty; it may also be noted that men have a sufficient natural instinct for what is true, and usually do arrive at the truth."* [V] (Bk I, Part 1) [AR]

Rhetoric is useful for four reasons (Bk I, Part 1) [AR]:

1. *"things that are true and things that are just have a natural tendency to prevail over their opposites"* [V], so if judges' decisions go wrong, *"the defeat must be due to the speakers themselves"* [V].
2. Before some audiences not even the exactest knowledge will make it easy to produce conviction, *"For argument based on knowledge implies instruction, and there are people whom one cannot instruct."* [V] Here we must use *"notions possessed by everybody"* [V].
3. We must be able to argue on opposite sides of a question, *"not in order that we may in practice employ it in both ways (for we must not make people believe what is wrong), but in order that we may see clearly what the facts are, and that, if another man argues unfairly, we on our part may be able to confute him"* [V].
4. It is absurd to be ashamed of being unable to defend oneself with one's limbs but not with *"speech and reason"* [V]. To the objection that the power can do great harm, the author answers that this charge may be made *"against all good things except virtue"* [V].

*"What makes a man a 'sophist' is not his faculty, but his moral purpose."* [V] (Bk I, Part 1) In rhetoric "rhetorician" may name either the speaker's knowledge of the art or his moral purpose; in dialectic, "sophist" names the moral purpose and "dialectician" the faculty. [AP]

### Bk I, Part 2: definition, the three modes of persuasion, enthymeme and example

Rhetoric is *"the faculty of observing in any given case the available means of persuasion"* [V]; every other art instructs or persuades about its own subject-matter, while rhetoric observes the means of persuasion *"on almost any subject presented to us"* [V] (Bk I, Part 2). [AR]

Some modes of persuasion belong to the art and some do not. The non-artistic ones are *"there at the outset-witnesses, evidence given under torture, written contracts, and so on"* [V]; the artistic ones are those we construct by the principles of rhetoric. *"The one kind has merely to be used, the other has to be invented."* [V] (Bk I, Part 2) [AP]

Three kinds of persuasion are furnished by the spoken word: the speaker's personal character, the audience's frame of mind, and the proof or apparent proof in the speech (quoted in the thesis above). On character: *"Persuasion is achieved by the speaker's personal character when the speech is so spoken as to make us think him credible."* [V] *"We believe good men more fully and more readily than others"* [V], absolutely so *"where exact certainty is impossible and opinions are divided"* [V]. *"This kind of persuasion, like the others, should be achieved by what the speaker says, not by what people think of his character before he begins to speak."* [V] Against writers who assume the speaker's personal goodness contributes nothing, *"his character may almost be called the most effective means of persuasion he possesses"* [V] (Bk I, Part 2). On emotion: *"Our judgements when we are pleased and friendly are not the same as when we are pained and hostile."* [V] (Bk I, Part 2) [AR]

The person in command of the three must be able *"(1) to reason logically, (2) to understand human character and goodness in their various forms, and (3) to understand the emotions-that is, to name them and describe them, to know their causes and the way in which they are excited"* [V]. Rhetoric therefore *"masquerades as political science"* [V], but is a branch of dialectic; neither is the scientific study of a separate subject: *"both are faculties for providing arguments"* [V] (Bk I, Part 2). [AR]

Proof works by example or enthymeme: *"I call the enthymeme a rhetorical syllogism, and the example a rhetorical induction."* [V] Everyone who persuades through proof uses one or the other: *"there is no other way"* [V]. Speeches relying on examples are as persuasive as the other kind, but enthymemes *"excite the louder applause"* [V] (Bk I, Part 2). [AR]

The theory concerns not what seems probable to an individual *"like Socrates or Hippias"* [V], but what seems probable *"to men of a given type"* [V]. *"The duty of rhetoric is to deal with such matters as we deliberate upon without arts or systems to guide us, in the hearing of persons who cannot take in at a glance a complicated argument, or follow a long chain of reasoning."* [V] Nobody who takes things to be incapable of being otherwise wastes time deliberating about them (Bk I, Part 2). Long chains from previous syllogisms are hard to follow, *"for we assume an audience of untrained thinkers"* [V]; premisses not generally accepted fail to win assent. [AR]

The enthymeme *"must consist of few propositions, fewer often than those which make up the normal syllogism. For if any of these propositions is a familiar fact, there is no need even to mention it; the hearer adds it himself."* [V] The worked example: to show Dorieus won a crowned contest, it is enough to say he won at the Olympic games without adding that the Olympic prize is a crown (Bk I, Part 2). [AE]

Few facts of the necessary type can form the basis of rhetorical syllogisms: *"For it is about our actions that we deliberate and inquire, and all our actions have a contingent character; hardly any of them are determined by necessity."* [V] The materials of enthymemes are Probabilities and Signs. A Probability is *"a thing that usually happens"* [V], but only within the contingent. Signs are infallible ("complete proof") or fallible. The author's illustrations (Bk I, Part 2) [AE]: a fever as a sign of illness, and giving milk as a sign of having lately borne a child, are infallible signs; Socrates being wise and just, offered as a sign that the wise are just, is refutable; and fast breathing as a sign of fever is refutable too. On the last: *"since a man may breathe hard without having a fever"* [V] (Bk I, Part 2).

The example's relation to what it proves is *"of part to part, or like to like"* [V]: Dionysius asking for a bodyguard is scheming to be a despot, as Peisistratus and Theagenes did before him, *"all these being instances of the one general principle, that a man who asks for a bodyguard is scheming to make himself a despot"* [V] (Bk I, Part 2). [AE]

The author marks a distinction he says *"has been wholly overlooked by almost everybody"* [V]: general Lines of Argument (such as "the more or less") apply equally to right conduct, natural science and politics; special Lines of Argument rest on propositions proper to one class of things. The better one selects special propositions, *"the nearer one comes, unconsciously, to setting up a science that is distinct from dialectic and rhetoric"* [V]. Most enthymemes rest on special lines (Bk I, Part 2). [AR]

### Bk I, Part 3: the three divisions of oratory

*"Rhetoric falls into three divisions, determined by the three classes of listeners to speeches."* [V] The hearer is either a judge of things past or future or an observer: an assembly member decides about future events, a juryman about past events, and *"those who merely decide on the orator's skill are observers"* [V]. Hence (1) political, (2) forensic and (3) *"the ceremonial oratory of display"* [V] (Bk I, Part 3). [AR]

Political speaking urges us to do or not to do something, and is used by private counsellors as well as public speakers; forensic speaking attacks or defends; ceremonial oratory praises or censures. Their times: political, the future; forensic, the past; ceremonial, *"properly speaking"* [V] the present. Their ends: the political orator establishes *"the expediency or the harmfulness of a proposed course of action"* [V]; parties in a law-case *"the justice or injustice of some action"* [V]; praise and attack aim at *"proving him worthy of honour or the reverse"* [V]; each treats other considerations as subsidiary (Bk I, Part 3). [AR]

The ends are shown by what speakers will concede: a litigant may admit he did a thing or did harm, *"But that he is guilty of injustice he will never admit"* [V]; political orators often concede anything short of admitting they recommend an inexpedient course, and *"The question whether it is not unjust for a city to enslave its innocent neighbours often does not trouble them at all"* [V]; praisers often praise a man for neglecting his own interest, as with Achilles, who championed Patroclus knowing it meant death (Bk I, Part 3). [AE]

All three kinds need propositions about the possible and impossible, about whether a thing has or will occur, and about greatness and smallness, *"both universal and particular"* [V] (Bk I, Part 3). [AP]

## Theme 2: Political oratory (Bk I, Parts 4–8)

### Bk I, Part 4: what the political orator counsels about

Counsel is given only on what may or may not take place, and not on things that happen naturally or by accident: *"Clearly counsel can only be given on matters about which people deliberate; matters, namely, that ultimately depend on ourselves, and which we have it in our power to set going."* [V] (Bk I, Part 4) A full classification of public business belongs to *"a more instructive art and a more real branch of knowledge"* [V]; rhetoric *"is a combination of the science of logic and of the ethical branch of politics"* [V], and the more we try to make dialectic and rhetoric sciences rather than *"practical faculties"* [V], the more we destroy their true nature (Bk I, Part 4). [AR]

The main subjects are *"some five in number: ways and means, war and peace, national defence, imports and exports, and legislation"* [V] (Bk I, Part 4). On each the speaker needs facts: revenue and expenditure (*"For men become richer not only by increasing their existing wealth but also by reducing their expenditure"* [V]), and knowledge of methods *"worked out in other lands"* [V]; military strength actual and potential, past wars and those of other countries, since *"similar causes are likely to have similar results"* [V]; the forts and lie of the country; food supply, imports and exports; and above all legislation, *"for it is on a country's laws that its whole welfare depends"* [V] (Bk I, Part 4). [AP]

Constitutions, except the best, are destroyed both by not being pushed far enough and by being pushed too far; democracy passes into oligarchy either way, as an aquiline or snub nose stops looking like a nose when too violently aquiline or snub (Bk I, Part 4). Books of travel and historians' researches help, *"But all this is the business of political science and not of rhetoric."* [V] (Bk I, Part 4) [AE]

### Bk I, Part 5: happiness and its constituents

Every individual and all men in common aim at an end, *"happiness and its constituents"* [V]; all advice to do or not to do concerns happiness and what makes for or against it (Bk I, Part 5). Happiness is defined four ways (prosperity with virtue; independence of life; secure enjoyment of maximum pleasure; good condition of property and body with power to guard and use them), and its constituents listed: good birth, friends, wealth, children, a happy old age, bodily excellences, fame, honour, good luck and virtue. The author defines each but virtue. Two of note: *"Wealth as a whole consists in using things rather than in owning them"* [V]; and a friend is *"one who will always try, for your sake, to do what he takes to be good for you"* [V] (Bk I, Part 5). Good luck covers good things *"contrary to reasonable expectation"* [V], as when a missile hits the next man and misses you. Virtue is deferred to the discussion of eulogy (Bk I, Part 5). [AP]

### Bk I, Part 6: the good and the useful

*"Now the political or deliberative orator's aim is utility: deliberation seeks to determine not ends but the means to ends, i.e. what it is most useful to do."* [V] (Bk I, Part 6) The author gives a set of definitions of a good thing (chosen for its own sake; that for whose sake we choose something else; what all things seek; what reason prescribes; what produces self-sufficiency; and what produces or maintains these) and a list of things admittedly good (happiness, the virtues, health, beauty, wealth, friends, honour, faculty of speech and action, the sciences and arts, life, justice) (Bk I, Part 6). [AP]

For disputed goods he lists lines of argument: that is good whose contrary is bad, or whose contrary benefits our enemies (with the caution that *"our interest is sometimes the same as that of our enemies"* [V]); what is not in excess; what has cost much labour or money; what most people seek; what is praised, especially by enemies; what a discerning person has favoured; what men deliberately choose; what is easily done; what is a man's own and exceptional (Bk I, Part 6). [AP]

### Bk I, Part 7: degrees of good

Because people often agree two things are useful but not which is more so, the author treats relative goodness. A greater number of goods is greater than one or fewer, if the smaller number is included in the count; if the largest member of one class surpasses the largest of another, the class surpasses the class; where one good is always accompanied by another but does not always accompany it, the first is greater than the second; what is a beginning or cause is greater (Bk I, Part 7). The same thing can be argued both ways: Leodamas, accusing Callistratus, said the prompter was more guilty than the doer; accusing Chabrias, that the doer was worse than the prompter, *"since there would have been no deed without some one to do it"* [V] (Bk I, Part 7). [AE]

Other lines: the rare is better than the plentiful, and reversely; what people of understanding would judge better is better; what a better man would choose is better (*"to suffer wrong rather than to do wrong"* [V]); the pleasanter, the nobler, the more lasting and secure; what is chosen by all; *"honour is, as it were, a measure of value"* [V]; things look better when divided into their parts, and the same effect comes from piling up facts in a climax; what aims at reality is better than what aims at appearance, and *"What a man wants to be is better than what a man wants to seem"* [V]; blinding a one-eyed man inflicts worse injury than half-blinding a man with two eyes (Bk I, Part 7). [AP]

### Bk I, Part 8: forms of government

*"The most important and effective qualification for success in persuading audiences and speaking well on public affairs is to understand all the forms of government and to discriminate their respective customs, institutions, and interests. For all men are persuaded by considerations of their interest, and their interest lies in the maintenance of the established order."* [V] (Bk I, Part 8) The four forms are democracy (offices by lot), oligarchy (property qualification), aristocracy (education laid down by law) and monarchy (kingship or tyranny). Their ends: *"The end of democracy is freedom; of oligarchy, wealth; of aristocracy, the maintenance of education and national institutions; of tyranny, the protection of the tyrant."* [V] (Bk I, Part 8) [AP]

Persuasion works *"not only by demonstrative but by ethical argument; it helps a speaker to convince us, if we believe that he has certain qualities himself, namely, goodness, or goodwill towards us, or both together"* [V]. So the speaker should know the moral qualities of each form of government, which are revealed, as an individual's are, *"in their deliberate acts of choice"* [V] (Bk I, Part 8). A detailed account is referred to the *Politics*. [AP]

## Theme 3: Ceremonial oratory (Bk I, Part 9)

### Bk I, Part 9: virtue, the noble, praise

Virtue and vice, the noble and the base are the objects of praise and blame, and studying them also shows *"how to make our hearers take the required view of our own characters-our second method of persuasion"* [V]. *"The ways in which to make them trust the goodness of other people are also the ways in which to make them trust our own."* [V] (Bk I, Part 9) [AR]

The Noble is what is desirable for its own sake and praiseworthy, or good and pleasant because good. Virtue is, according to the usual view, *"a faculty of providing and preserving good things"* [V], with forms justice, courage, temperance, magnificence, magnanimity, liberality, gentleness, prudence and wisdom; if virtue is a faculty of beneficence, the highest kinds must be those most useful to others, so men honour most the just and courageous. Prudence is the virtue of the understanding *"which enables men to come to wise decisions about the relation to happiness of the goods and evils"* [V] (Bk I, Part 9). Noble acts include those done for others' sake, those whose reward is honour, and those whose advantage outlives the doer. [AP]

In praise or blame the speaker is to treat qualities closely allied to a man's actual ones as identical with them, so the cautious man is called cold-blooded, the stupid man an honest fellow, the passionate man "outspoken", rashness courage and extravagance generosity. The same method, the author adds, *"enables an advocate to draw a misleading inference from the motive"* [V]: if a man runs into danger needlessly, much more will he do so in a noble cause (Bk I, Part 9). [AR]

The audience must be taken into account: *"for, as Socrates used to say, 'it is not difficult to praise the Athenians to an Athenian audience.'"* [V] Whatever the audience esteems should be represented as noble, *"After all, people regard the two things as much the same"* [V] (Bk I, Part 9). Praise addresses actions as intentional; to prove intent, cite repeated actions of the same kind. Praise and counsel convert into each other: the suggestion "A man should be proud not of what he owes to fortune but of what he owes to himself" becomes praise as "Since he is proud ...". *"Consequently, whenever you want to praise any one, think what you would urge people to do; and when you want to urge the doing of anything, think what you would praise a man for having done."* [V] (Bk I, Part 9) [AR]

Heightening the effect of praise: show he was the only one or first, the occasion was unlooked-for, he achieved it often; compare him with famous men, or at least with others. Of the common lines of argument, *"this 'heightening of effect' is most suitable for declamations"* [V]; examples suit deliberative speeches, *"for we judge of future events by divination from past events"* [V]; enthymemes suit forensic speeches, where *"it is our doubts about past events that most admit of arguments"* [V] (Bk I, Part 9). Censure needs no separate treatment: it is made from the contraries. [AR]

## Theme 4: Forensic oratory (Bk I, Parts 10–15)

### Bk I, Part 10: wrong-doing and the seven causes of action

Accusation and defence need three things ascertained: the incentives to wrong-doing, the state of mind of wrongdoers, and the kind of persons wronged (Bk I, Part 10). *"We may describe 'wrong-doing' as injury voluntarily inflicted contrary to law."* [V] Law is special (the written law of a community) or general (*"all those unwritten principles which are supposed to be acknowledged everywhere"* [V]). We act voluntarily when we act *"consciously and without constraint"* [V]; not all voluntary acts are deliberate, but all deliberate acts are conscious. The causes of deliberately intending harmful acts contrary to law are vice and lack of self-control, and *"any wrong that any one does to others corresponds to his particular faults of character"* [V] (Bk I, Part 10). [AR]

The prosecutor must consider which of all the aims that induce wrong-doing affect his adversary, *"while the defendant must consider how many, and which, do not affect him"* [V]. Every action is or is not due to the person himself. Those not due to him are due to chance, nature or compulsion; those due to him to habit or to rational or irrational craving (wish, or anger and appetite). *"Thus every action must be due to one or other of seven causes: chance, nature, compulsion, habit, reasoning, anger, or appetite."* [V] (Bk I, Part 10) [AR]

The author rejects further distinction by age, wealth or moral state as causes: young men have hot tempers and strong appetites, *"still, it is not through youth that they act accordingly, but through anger or appetite"* [V]; the poor act from appetite for money, *"but here, again, their actions will be due not to wealth or poverty but to appetite"* [V]. Yet *"we must consider what kinds of actions and of people usually go together"* [V]: age and justice make a difference where complexion and height do not (Bk I, Part 10). [AR]

Each cause is defined. Chance covers things *"whose cause cannot be determined, that have no purpose, and that happen neither always nor usually nor in any fixed way"* [V]; nature, things with *"a fixed and internal cause"* [V]; compulsion, things done *"contrary to the desire or reason of the doer, yet through his own agency"* [V]; habit, what men do *"because they have often done them before"* [V]; reasoning, actions done because they appear useful; anger, acts of revenge; appetite, actions that appear pleasant. *"Revenge and punishment are different things. Punishment is inflicted for the sake of the person punished; revenge for that of the punisher, to satisfy his feelings."* [V] All voluntary actions *"must either be or seem to be either good or pleasant"* [V] (Bk I, Part 10). The part closes: *"Our various definitions must be regarded as adequate, even if they are not exact, provided they are clear."* [V] (Bk I, Part 10) [AP]

### Bk I, Part 11: the pleasant

*"We may lay it down that Pleasure is a movement, a movement by which the soul as a whole is consciously brought into its normal state of being; and that Pain is the opposite."* [V] (Bk I, Part 11) From this the author derives a long list: habits are pleasant, since *"as soon as a thing has become habitual, it is virtually natural"* [V]; what is compulsory is painful, so *"all acts of concentration, strong effort, and strain are necessarily painful"* [V] unless we are accustomed to them; ease, rest and sleep are pleasant; desires are irrational (bodily) or rational (*"there are many things we desire to see or get because we have been told of them and induced to believe them good"* [V]) (Bk I, Part 11). [AP]

Pleasure attaches to memory and expectation as well as present perception; some things not pleasant at the time are pleasant to remember *"provided that their results have subsequently proved noble and good"* [V]. Revenge, victory, honour from good judges, being loved, being admired, change (*"change means an approach to nature"* [V]), learning and wondering (pleasant "as a rule"), conferring and receiving benefits, imitation (*"the spectator draws inferences ('That is a so-and-so') and thus learns something fresh"* [V]), what is our own, completing what is defective, being thought wise, and the ludicrous are all pleasant (Bk I, Part 11). The ludicrous is referred to *"the treatise on the Art of Poetry"* [V]. [AP]

### Bk I, Part 12: the states of mind of wrongdoers and their victims

Wrongdoers *"must themselves suppose that the thing can be done, and done by them"* [V]: that they will not be found out, or will escape punishment, or that the penalty will be less than the gain (Bk I, Part 12). They feel safe if they have eloquence, practical ability, legal experience, friends or money; if their appearance contradicts the charge (*"a weakling is unlikely to be charged with violent assault"* [V]); with public and open injuries, and crimes too great to be suspected: *"For all men guard against ordinary offences, just as they guard against ordinary diseases; but no one takes precautions against a disease that nobody has ever had."* [V] (Bk I, Part 12) [AP]

They may count on staving off trial, or on gain that is great, certain or immediate against a penalty that is small, uncertain or distant. Weak-willed people may be drawn by immediate pleasure or gain with later pain or loss; self-controlled and sensible people by immediate pain and loss with later, longer-lasting pleasure and profit. They may also count on making the act appear *"due to chance, or to necessity, or to natural causes, or to habit: in fact, to put it generally, as if you had failed to do right rather than actually done wrong"* [V] (Bk I, Part 12). Their victims are those who have what they want; the trustful; the easy-going; those often or never wronged before; those unpopular or without friends; foreigners and small farmers who will *"settle for a trifle"* [V]; those who have themselves wronged others; and those whose wronging lets the wrongdoer do *"many righteous acts"* [V], as Jason the Thessalian argued (Bk I, Part 12). The kinds of wrong done include those done universally or commonly, which the wrongdoer expects to be forgiven; those easily kept dark; those the victim is ashamed to speak of; and trifling ones that it would seem litigious to prosecute. [AP]

### Bk I, Part 13: law, being wronged, equity

Just and unjust actions are defined relative to two kinds of law and two classes of persons. *"Particular law is that which each community lays down and applies to its own members: this is partly written and partly unwritten. Universal law is the law of Nature."* [V] The author cites Sophocles' Antigone on the burial of Polyneices as just by nature, Empedocles on killing no living creature, and Alcidamas (the sentence breaks off in the tape) (Bk I, Part 13). [BT] Wrongs affect either the community (the man who avoids army service) or a definite person (adultery, assault). To be wronged *"a man must (1) suffer actual harm, (2) suffer it against his will"* [V] (Bk I, Part 13). [AP]

A defendant will often admit an act but not the prosecutor's label for it: that he took a thing but not that he "stole" it; that he struck first but not that he committed "outrage"; that he communicated with the enemy but not that he committed "treason". So we must be able to distinguish what theft, outrage or adultery is. *"It is deliberate purpose that constitutes wickedness and criminal guilt, and such names as 'outrage' or 'theft' imply deliberate purpose as well as the mere action."* [V] (Bk I, Part 13) [AR]

Unwritten conduct is of two kinds: exceptional goodness or badness visited with praise or censure, and equity, *"the sort of justice which goes beyond the written law"* [V]. Its existence is partly unintended by legislators, where they have noticed no defect in the law, and partly intended, where they cannot define things exactly and must legislate *"as if that held good always which in fact only holds good usually"* [V], or because cases are endless: *"a lifetime would be too short to make out a complete list"* [V] of weapons that may wound. A man who strikes with a finger-ring on his hand is guilty of a criminal act *"according to the unwritten words of the law"* [V] (so the tape prints it) but *"innocent really, and it is equity that declares him to be so"* [V] (Bk I, Part 13). [AR]

Equity distinguishes three kinds of act: *"A 'misfortune' is an act, not due to moral badness, that has unexpected results: an 'error of judgement' is an act, also not due to moral badness, that has results that might have been expected: a 'criminal act' has results that might have been expected, but is due to moral badness"* [V] (Bk I, Part 13). [AR]

> "Equity bids us be merciful to the weakness of human nature; to think less about the laws than about the man who framed them, and less about what he said than about what he meant; not to consider the actions of the accused so much as his intentions, nor this or that detail so much as the whole story; to ask not what a man is now but what he has always or usually been." (Bk I, Part 13)

It also bids us *"remember benefits rather than injuries, and benefits received rather than benefits conferred; to be patient when we are wronged; to settle a dispute by negotiation and not by force; to prefer arbitration to motion-for an arbitrator goes by the equity of a case, a judge by the strict law"* [V] (Bk I, Part 13). [AR]

### Bk I, Part 14: the comparative badness of wrongs

*"The worse of two acts of wrong done to others is that which is prompted by the worse disposition."* [V] So the most trifling acts may be the worst, as when Callistratus charged Melanopus with cheating the temple-builders of three consecrated half-obols: *"there is no crime that a man who has stolen three consecrated half-obols would shrink from committing"* [V] (Bk I, Part 14). [AE] A wrong may also be worse by the greater harm, when no punishment is adequate, when the harm is incurable, when the wrongdoer was first or only, when it led to new laws and prisons, when it is brutal or deliberate, when it breaks many obligations at once or is committed in a law-court, when it wrongs a benefactor, or when it breaks the unwritten laws; though *"It may however be argued otherwise, that the crime is worse which breaks the written laws"* [V] (Bk I, Part 14). [AP]

### Bk I, Part 15: the non-technical means of persuasion

The non-technical means are *"specially characteristic of forensic oratory. They are five in number: laws, witnesses, contracts, tortures, oaths."* [V] (Bk I, Part 15) For each, the author gives arguments for whichever side it suits. [AR]

*Laws.* If the written law tells against us, appeal to universal law and equity, argue the juror's oath to give *"my verdict according to honest opinion"* [V] means not simply following the letter of the written law, that equity is permanent and written laws change, that a law contradicts another or itself, is ambiguous, or has outlived its situation. If it supports us, argue that the oath protects judges from perjury, not licenses verdicts against the law, an argument that likens not using the laws to having no laws at all (the tape's wording is garbled at this point, "as ahas"; see the integrity notes), and that *"it does not pay to try to be cleverer than the doctor: for less harm comes from the doctor's mistakes than from the growing habit of disobeying authority"* [V] (Bk I, Part 15). [AP]

*Witnesses.* Ancient witnesses are the poets and notable persons whose judgements are known, and concern past events; for future events one appeals to soothsayers; proverbs are also a form of evidence; recent witnesses are well-known people who have given opinions, and those who share the risk of punishment if their evidence is false. The latter *"are valid witnesses to the fact that an action was or was not done, that something is or is not the case; they are not valid witnesses to the quality of an action, to its being just or unjust, useful or harmful"* [V]; on quality, *"the opinion of detached persons is highly trustworthy"* [V], and ancient witnesses most of all, *"since they cannot be corrupted"* [V] (Bk I, Part 15). Without witnesses, argue that the judges must decide from probability, *"that probabilities cannot be bribed to mislead the court; and that probabilities are never convicted of perjury"* [V]; if you have witnesses and your opponent has none, argue that probabilities *"cannot be put on their trial"* [V] (Bk I, Part 15). Evidence may concern fact or character, so *"we need never be at a loss for useful evidence"* [V]. [AP]

*Contracts.* Their credit depends on the character of the signatories and custodians. In favour: a contract is a special law, and *"if these lose their binding force, human intercourse ceases to exist"* [V]. Against: use the arguments against a bad law; the judge as umpire must ask *"where justice lies, and not what this or that document means"* [V]; contracts may be products of fraud or force (Bk I, Part 15). [AP]

*Torture.* Great weight is often attached to it *"because it is in a sense compulsory"* [V]. Against it, one may say *"what is true of torture of every kind alike, that people under its compulsion tell lies quite as often as they tell the truth, sometimes persistently refusing to tell the truth, sometimes recklessly making a false charge in order to be let off sooner"* [V] (Bk I, Part 15). A further bracketed passage in the tape says no trust can be placed in evidence under torture. [AP]

*Oaths.* A fourfold division (offer and accept, neither, offer only, accept only), plus an oath already sworn. The author supplies the argument for each position; for a contradictory earlier oath of one's own, argue that it is not perjury, *"since perjury is a crime, and a crime must be a voluntary action"* [V], so that *"perjury depends on the intention and not on the spoken words"* [V] (Bk I, Part 15). [AP]

## Theme 5: Character and the emotions (Bk II, Parts 1–17)

### Bk II, Part 1: why character and emotion matter; three sources of credibility

*"But since rhetoric exists to affect the giving of decisions-the hearers decide between one political speaker and another, and a legal verdict is a decision-the orator must not only try to make the argument of his speech demonstrative and worthy of belief; he must also make his own character look right and put his hearers, who are to decide, into the right frame of mind."* [V] (Bk II, Part 1) The speaker's character is particularly important in political speaking, and the audience's frame of mind in lawsuits. *"When people are feeling friendly and placable, they think one sort of thing; when they are feeling angry or hostile, they think either something totally different or the same thing with a different intensity"* [V] (Bk II, Part 1). [AR]

Three things inspire confidence in the orator's character *"apart from any proof of it: good sense, good moral character, and goodwill"* [V]. The author derives them from the causes of bad advice:

> "Men either form a false opinion through want of good sense; or they form a true opinion, but because of their moral badness do not say what they really think; or finally, they are both sensible and upright, but not well disposed to their hearers, and may fail in consequence to recommend what they know to be the best course." (Bk II, Part 1)

*"These are the only possible cases. It follows that any one who is thought to have all three of these good qualities will inspire trust in his audience."* [V] (Bk II, Part 1) Good sense and goodness are shown by the analysis of goodness already given; goodwill belongs to the emotions. [AR]

*"The Emotions are all those feelings that so change men as to affect their judgements, and that are also attended by pain or pleasure."* [V] Each is treated under three heads: the state of mind of those who feel it, the people towards whom it is felt, and the grounds. *"It is not enough to know one or even two of these points; unless we know all three, we shall be unable to arouse anger in any one."* [V] (Bk II, Part 1) [AR]

### Bk II, Part 2: anger

*"Anger may be defined as an impulse, accompanied by pain, to a conspicuous revenge for a conspicuous slight directed without justification towards what concerns oneself or towards what concerns one's friends."* [V] (Bk II, Part 2) It is felt towards an individual, *"e.g. Cleon, and not 'man' in general"* [V], and is attended by the pleasure of expected revenge. *"Now slighting is the actively entertained opinion of something as obviously of no importance."* [V] It has three kinds: contempt, spite (thwarting another's wishes not to gain but to prevent his gaining) and insolence (shaming the victim *"simply for the pleasure involved"* [V]) (Bk II, Part 2). One sort of insolence *"is to rob people of the honour due to them"* [V]. [AR]

Frame of mind: anyone in pain and aiming at something is prone to anger, *"especially against those who slight their present distress"* [V]; and *"a quite unexpected evil is specially painful"* [V] (Bk II, Part 2). Objects: those who mock us; who show contempt for what we care most about, especially where we doubt ourselves; friends more than others; those who change their treatment of us; who fail to return kindness; inferiors who oppose us; friends who do not perceive our needs; those who rejoice at our misfortunes; those indifferent to the pain they give us, *"this is why we get angry with bringers of bad news"* [V]; those who slight us before rivals, those we admire, those we wish to admire us, those we revere, or those who revere us; those who reply with levity when we are serious; and those who forget: *"Forgetfulness, too, causes anger, as when our own names are forgotten, trifling as this may be; since forgetfulness is felt to be another sign that we are being slighted"* [V] (Bk II, Part 2). The orator will bring hearers into a frame of mind disposed to anger and represent adversaries as open to such charges. [AP]

### Bk II, Part 3: calmness

*"Growing calm may be defined as a settling down or quieting of anger."* [V] Since slighting is voluntary, we are calm towards those who did it involuntarily or meant the opposite; towards those who treat themselves as they treated us; and *"towards those who admit their fault and are sorry: since we accept their grief at what they have done as satisfaction, and cease to be angry"* [V] (Bk II, Part 3). The punishment of servants shows this: those who deny their offence are punished all the more, because *"it is shameless to deny what is obvious, and those who are shameless towards us slight us"* [V]. We are calm towards those who humble themselves, who are serious when we are serious, who have done us more kindness than we them, and towards people we fear or respect (Bk II, Part 3). [AR]

The calm frame of mind is the opposite of the angry: amusement, prosperity, inoffensive pleasure, justifiable hope. *"Also when time has passed and their anger is no longer fresh, for time puts an end to anger."* [V] Anger spent on one person ends anger at another: Philocrates, asked when he would defend himself, answered "When I see someone else calumniated"; Ergophilus was acquitted because Callisthenes had been condemned the day before (Bk II, Part 3). [AE] We are calm if we feel we are suffering justly, *"for anger is not excited by what is just"* [V], and towards those who cannot know of our anger, including the dead. To calm others, represent those they are angry with *"as formidable, or as worthy of reverence, or as benefactors, or as involuntary agents, or as much distressed at what they have done"* [V] (Bk II, Part 3). [AP]

### Bk II, Part 4: friendship and enmity

*"We may describe friendly feeling towards any one as wishing for him what you believe to be good things, not for your own sake but for his, and being inclined, so far as you can, to bring these things about."* [V] (Bk II, Part 4) A friend shares our pleasure and pain *"for your sake and for no other reason"* [V]. We feel friendly to those who have treated us or those we care for well, provided they did so for our sake, to friends' friends and enemies' enemies, to the liberal, brave and just, to the good-tempered, *"and those who are not too ready to show us our mistakes"* [V], to those who can take and make a joke, who praise qualities we are unsure we have, who *"do not nurse grudges or store up grievances, but are always ready to make friends again"* [V], to those like ourselves who do not compete with us (*"Potter to potter and builder to builder begrudge their reward"* [V]), to those *"who are honest with us, including those who will tell us of their own weak points"* [V], and to those *"with whom we do not feel frightened or uncomfortable-nobody can like a man of whom he feels frightened"* [V] (Bk II, Part 4). Friendship is caused by *"doing kindnesses; doing them unasked; and not proclaiming the fact when they are done"* [V]. [AP]

Enmity may be produced by anger, spite or calumny, and unlike anger may arise from what we take to be a person's character alone. *"Anger is always concerned with individuals-a Callias or a Socrates-whereas hatred is directed also against classes"* [V]. *"Moreover, anger can be cured by time; but hatred cannot."* [V] The angry man wants his victim to feel; the hater would have him cease to exist (Bk II, Part 4). The orator can thus prove people friends or enemies, make them out to be so, refute claims to be so, and attribute an action to anger or hatred *"whichever of these we prefer"* [V]. [AR]

### Bk II, Part 5: fear and confidence

*"Fear may be defined as a pain or disturbance due to a mental picture of some destructive or painful evil in the future."* [V] Only evils that are great and near: *"we all know we shall die, but we are not troubled thereby, because death is not close at hand"* [V]. Danger is defined from this: *"the approach of what is terrible is just what we mean by 'danger'"* [V]. (Bk II, Part 5) Fearful are the enmity and anger of the powerful, injustice and outraged virtue in possession of power, those who know of something horrible we have done, rivals for something we cannot both have at once, and of enemies *"not the passionate and outspoken whom we have to fear, but the quiet, dissembling, unscrupulous"* [V]. *"All terrible things are more terrible if they give us no chance of retrieving a blunder"* [V] (Bk II, Part 5). [AP]

Fear is felt only by those who think something likely to happen to them, from particular persons, in a particular form, at a particular time; not by those who are, or think they are, in great prosperity and consequently become insolent, contemptuous and reckless, nor by those past hope: *"This appears from the fact that fear sets us thinking what can be done, which of course nobody does when things are hopeless."* [V] So the orator who wants the audience frightened must make them feel in danger, *"pointing out that it has happened to others who were stronger than they are"* [V], and to people like them, *"at the hands of unexpected people, in an unexpected form, and at an unexpected time"* [V] (Bk II, Part 5). [AR]

Confidence is the opposite of fear, *"the expectation associated with a mental picture of the nearness of what keeps us safe and the absence or remoteness of what is terrible"* [V]. We feel it if we can take many or important steps, or both, to cure or prevent trouble, have not wronged others, have no strong rivals. People face danger calmly for two reasons: *"they may have no experience of it, or they may have means to deal with it"* [V], as at sea some are confident from no experience of bad weather and others because experience gives them the means of dealing with it (Bk II, Part 5). [AR]

### Bk II, Part 6: shame and shamelessness

*"Shame may be defined as pain or disturbance in regard to bad things, whether present, past, or future, which seem likely to involve us in discredit; and shamelessness as contempt or indifference in regard to these same bad things."* [V] (Bk II, Part 6) Shameful are things due to moral badness: cowardice, injustice about money, licentiousness, petty greed, meanness, flattery, effeminacy, ingratitude, and *"talking incessantly about yourself, making loud professions, and appropriating the merits of others; for this is due to boastfulness"* [V]. Also lacking a share in the honourable things shared by everyone else, or by all or nearly all of those like ourselves, all the more *"if it is seen to be our own fault"* [V] (Bk II, Part 6). [AP]

Since shame concerns opinion, we feel it before *"those whose opinion of us matters to us"* [V]: those who admire us, whom we admire, by whom we wish to be admired, with whom we compete, and whose opinion we respect. *"And we feel more shame about a thing if it is done openly, before all men's eyes. Hence the proverb, 'shame dwells in the eyes'."* [V] We feel it before those always with us, before those likely to tell others, before satirists, before those who have not yet seen us fail. *"nor are we ashamed of the same things before intimates as before strangers, but before the former of what seem genuine faults, before the latter of what seem conventional ones"* [V] (Bk II, Part 6). [AP] Cydias told the Athenians to imagine the Greeks standing around them, *"actually seeing the way they voted and not merely going to hear about it afterwards"* [V] (Bk II, Part 6). [AE]

### Bk II, Part 7: kindness and unkindness

Kindness is *"helpfulness towards some one in need, not in return for anything, nor for the advantage of the helper himself, but for that of the person helped"* [V]. Kindness is great if the person helped is in great need, needs something important and hard to get, or needs it at an important and difficult crisis; or if the helper is the only, first or chief person to help (Bk II, Part 7). To eliminate the idea of kindness, maintain that the helpers acted for their own interest, by accident, under force, or *"merely returning one"* [V]; or that a smaller service had been refused, or an equal one given to enemies (Bk II, Part 7). [AP]

### Bk II, Part 8: pity

*"Pity may be defined as a feeling of pain caused by the sight of some evil, destructive or painful, which befalls one who does not deserve it, and which we might expect to befall ourselves or some friend of ours, and moreover to befall us soon."* [V] (Bk II, Part 8) It is not felt by the completely ruined, nor by those who think themselves immensely fortunate, nor by the panic-stricken, *"only those feel pity who are between these two extremes"* [V]. We must also believe in the goodness of at least some people (Bk II, Part 8). [AR]

We pity those we know, unless very closely related: Amasis did not weep at his son led to death but wept at a friend begging, *"the latter sight was pitiful, the former terrible, and the terrible is different from the pitiful; it tends to cast out pity"* [V]. We pity those like us, and what is near in time; so speakers who use *"suitable gestures, tones, dress, and dramatic action generally, are especially successful in exciting pity: they thus put the disasters before our eyes"* [V]. Most piteous is when the victims are of noble character (Bk II, Part 8). [AR]

### Bk II, Part 9: indignation

Indignation is opposite to pity: *"Pain at unmerited good fortune is, in one sense, opposite to pain at unmerited bad fortune, and is due to the same moral qualities."* [V] Envy differs from indignation: it is pain at the prosperity *"of people who are like us or equal with us"* [V], not of the undeserving. All these feelings *"tend to prevent pity"* [V] and are useful for neutralising an appeal to pity (Bk II, Part 9). *"Indignation is pain caused by the sight of undeserved good fortune."* [V] It is roused by wealth and power, more against the newly rich than old wealth, and by anyone getting *"what is not appropriate for him"* [V]. It is felt by those who deserve and have the greatest goods, by the good and honest, and by the ambitious; *"Hence servile, worthless, unambitious persons are not inclined to Indignation"* [V] (Bk II, Part 9). [AR]

### Bk II, Part 10: envy

*"Envy is pain at the sight of such good fortune as consists of the good things already mentioned; we feel it towards our equals; not with the idea of getting something for ourselves, but because the other people have it."* [V] (Bk II, Part 10) It is felt by those who fall a little short of everything, by the ambitious, by those who profess wisdom, by the small-minded; towards those near us in time, place, age or reputation, and towards competitors (*"Potter against potter"* [V]). *"We also envy those whose possession of or success in a thing is a reproach to us: these are our neighbours and equals; for it is clear that it is our own fault we have missed the good thing in question"* [V] (Bk II, Part 10). If judges are put into an envious frame of mind and those claiming pity are of the kind described in the account of envy, the latter will win no pity. [AP]

### Bk II, Part 11: emulation

*"Emulation is pain caused by seeing the presence, in persons whose nature is like our own, of good things that are highly valued and are possible for ourselves to acquire; but it is felt not because others have these goods, but because we have not got them ourselves."* [V] It is *"a good feeling felt by good persons, whereas envy is a bad feeling felt by bad persons. Emulation makes us take steps to secure the good things in question, envy makes us take steps to stop our neighbour having them."* [V] (Bk II, Part 11) It is felt by the young and high-minded; its objects are those with courage, wisdom and office. Contempt is its opposite. This completes the account of the emotions (Bk II, Part 11). [AR]

### Bk II, Parts 12–14: character by age

The author describes character *"in relation to the emotions and moral qualities"* [V] by ages (youth, prime, old age) and by fortune (Bk II, Part 12). [AP]

The young have strong, changeable passions; they are hot-tempered, love honour and victory more than money; *"They trust others readily, because they have not yet often been cheated"* [V]; they live in expectation rather than memory; they are more courageous than older men, and shy; choose the noble over the useful, and are fond of companions. *"All their mistakes are in the direction of doing things excessively and vehemently."* [V] *"They think they know everything, and are always quite sure about it; this, in fact, is why they overdo everything."* [V] (Bk II, Part 12) [AP]

Elderly men may be said to be formed, for the most part, of the contrary: *"they have often been taken in, and often made mistakes; and life on the whole is a bad business. The result is that they are sure about nothing and under-do everything."* [V] They "think" but never "know", always adding *"a 'possibly'or a 'perhaps'"* [V] (tape spacing). They are cynical, distrustful, small-minded, ungenerous, cowardly, fond of life and of themselves; they guide their lives *"too much by considerations of what is useful and too little by what is noble"* [V]; they live by memory, are querulous, and pity out of weakness (Bk II, Part 13). *"People always think well of speeches adapted to, and reflecting, their own character: and we can now see how to compose our speeches so as to adapt both them and ourselves to our audiences."* [V] (Bk II, Part 13) [AR]

Men in their prime lie between, free from both extremes: *"They neither trust everybody nor distrust everybody, but judge people correctly."* [V] *"The body is in its prime from thirty to five-and-thirty; the mind about forty-nine."* [V] (Bk II, Part 14) [AP]

### Bk II, Parts 15–17: character by fortune

Good birth makes men more ambitious and disdainful; it must be distinguished from *"nobility, which means being true to the family nature-a quality not usually found in the well-born"* [V]; now and then, where the stock is good, exceptional men are produced for a while, *"and then decadence sets in"* [V] (Bk II, Part 15). [AP]

Wealth makes men insolent, arrogant, luxurious and ostentatious, imagining *"there is nothing it cannot buy"* [V]. *"In a word, the type of character produced by wealth is that of a prosperous fool."* [V] The newly enriched have these qualities worse, having *"no education in riches"* [V] (Bk II, Part 16). [AP]

Power shares some of wealth's traits and is better in others: those in power are more ambitious and manly; *"Responsibility makes them more serious: they have to keep paying attention to the duties their position involves."* [V] They are *"dignified rather than arrogant"* [V]; if they do wrong, they do it on a great scale. Good fortune makes men more supercilious and more reckless, but also pious (Bk II, Part 17). The opposite types (poor, unfortunate, powerless) follow by contraries. [AP]

## Theme 6: Arguments common to all oratory (Bk II, Parts 18–26)

### Bk II, Part 18: the use of persuasive speech

*"The use of persuasive speech is to lead to decisions. (When we know a thing, and have decided about it, there is no further use in speaking about it.)"* [V] This holds when addressing a single person, *"as when we scold a man for his conduct or try to change his views"* [V]; *"we may say, without qualification, that any one is your judge whom you have to persuade"* [V]. It holds against a mere proposition as against an opponent, and for ceremonial onlookers, though strictly the judge is the one who decides an issue of public controversy (Bk II, Part 18). [AR]

All orators use the common topics of the Possible and Impossible, of past and future fact, and of Size. Amplification is most appropriate to ceremonial speeches, the Past to forensic, Possibility and the Future to political (Bk II, Part 18). [AP]

### Bk II, Part 19: possible, past fact, future fact, size

Lines for the possible: if one contrary is possible so is the other; if the harder is possible so is the easier; if the beginning so the end, and the reverse; if the parts so the whole; *"That anything is possible the first step in whose production depends on men or things which we can compel or persuade to produce it, by our greater strength, our control of them, or our friendship with them."* [V]; what can be produced without art can be produced more certainly with it; what inferior people can do, their betters can (Bk II, Part 19). [AP]

Past fact: if the less likely happened, the more likely did; *"That if a man had the power and the wish to do a thing, he has done it; for every one does do whatever he intends to do whenever he can do it, there being nothing to stop him."* [V] If a thing that naturally precedes has happened, the other has (*"if it has lightened, it has also thundered"* [V]); *"Of all these sequences some are inevitable and some merely usual."* [V] (Bk II, Part 19) Future fact: a thing will be done if there is power and wish, or power with craving, anger or calculation. If the means to an end have occurred, the end is likely to occur; the author's illustration is *"if there is a foundation, there will be a house"* [V] (Bk II, Part 19). [AP]

Size draws on the earlier account of relative goods; *"To go further than this, and try to establish abstract laws of greatness and superiority, is to argue without an object; in practical life, particular facts count more than generalizations."* [V] (Bk II, Part 19) [AR]

### Bk II, Part 20: argument by example

The common forms are Example and Enthymeme, *"for the 'Maxim' is part of an enthymeme"* [V]. Example *"has the nature of induction, which is the foundation of reasoning"* [V]. It has two varieties: mention of actual past facts, and invention by the speaker, which is either the illustrative parallel or the fable (Bk II, Part 20). [AR]

The author's illustrations: Darius and Xerxes each seized Egypt before crossing to Greece, so the present king must not be let seize Egypt; Socrates' parallel that choosing officials by lot is like choosing athletes or a steersman by lot, *"and not the man who knows most about it"* [V]; Stesichorus' fable of the horse who let a man bridle him to get revenge on a stag and became the man's slave; Aesop's fable of the fox who declined to have her full fleas removed lest hungry ones come (Bk II, Part 20). [AE]

Fables suit popular assemblies and are comparatively easy to invent, but *"it is more valuable for the political speaker to supply them by quoting what has actually happened, since in most respects the future will be like what the past has been"* [V] (Bk II, Part 20). Where enthymeme is unavailable, argue by example; where it is available, examples should follow as supplementary evidence, like witnesses, and *"even a single witness will serve if he is a good one"* [V]; put first, examples give *"an inductive air, which only rarely suits the conditions of speech-making"* [V] and must be many (Bk II, Part 20). [AR]

### Bk II, Part 21: maxims

A maxim is a general statement *"only about questions of practical conduct, courses of conduct to be chosen or avoided"* [V]; the premisses or conclusions of enthymemes, taken apart, are roughly maxims (Bk II, Part 21). Maxims with no supplement suit statements already known or clear at a glance; those with a supplement are part of an enthymeme or have its character with the reason implied, and these *"are reckoned the best"* [V]. Disputed or paradoxical maxims need their reason. [AP]

*"The use of Maxims is appropriate only to elderly men, and in handling subjects in which the speaker is experienced."* [V] For a young man it is unbecoming; on subjects outside one's experience, *"silly and ill-bred"* [V] (Bk II, Part 21). Even hackneyed maxims serve, *"just because they are commonplace, every one seems to agree with them, and therefore they are taken for truth"* [V]. [AR]

Two advantages. First, hearers *"love to hear him succeed in expressing as a universal truth the opinions which they hold themselves about particular cases"* [V], so *"The orator has therefore to guess the subjects on which his hearers really hold views already, and what those views are, and then must express, as general truths, these same views on these same subjects."* [V] Second, more important, maxims invest a speech with moral character, *"because the utterance of them amounts to a general declaration of moral principles"* [V] (Bk II, Part 21). [AR]

### Bk II, Part 22: looking for enthymemes

*"Thus we must not carry its reasoning too far back, or the length of our argument will cause obscurity: nor must we put in all the steps that lead to our conclusion, or we shall waste words in saying what is manifest."* [V] This simplicity is why the uneducated are more effective with popular audiences: *"Educated men lay down broad general principles; uneducated men argue from common knowledge and draw obvious conclusions."* [V] Start only from opinions *"accepted by our judges or by those whose authority they recognize"* [V], and argue from probabilities as well as certainties (Bk II, Part 22). [AR]

*"Whether our argument concerns public affairs or some other subject, we must know some, if not all, of the facts about the subject on which we are to speak and argue. Otherwise we can have no materials out of which to construct arguments."* [V] To advise the Athenians on war, one must know their strength, revenues, friends and enemies and past wars; to eulogise them, Salamis and Marathon (Bk II, Part 22). [AE] Prepare a selection of arguments in advance, then think out arguments for special needs *"by keeping our eyes on the actual facts of the subject we have to speak on"* [V]: *"for the more actual facts we have at our command, the more easily we prove our case; and the more closely they bear on the subject, the more they will seem to belong to that speech only instead of being commonplaces"* [V]. Praise of Achilles for being human or joining the Trojan expedition fits Diomede as well; the special facts are those *"true of Achilles alone"* [V] (Bk II, Part 22). [AR]

There are two kinds of enthymeme: *"The demonstrative enthymeme is formed by the conjunction of compatible propositions; the refutative, by the conjunction of incompatible propositions."* [V] (Bk II, Part 22) [AP]

### Bk II, Part 23: the lines of argument

The author lists lines of argument for enthymemes, numbered 1–27 in the tape (with irregularities noted in the integrity notes). In summary (Bk II, Part 23) [AP]:

1. From opposites: does the opposite have the opposite quality? (*"Temperance is beneficial; for licentiousness is hurtful"* [V], given in single quotes in the tape.)
2. From modifications of the key-word ("just" does not always mean "beneficial").
3. From correlative ideas, with a caution: *"It may be just that A should be treated in a certain way, and yet not just that he should be so treated by B. Hence you must ask yourself two distinct questions: (1) Is it right that A should be thus treated? (2) Is it right that B should thus treat him?"* [V]
4. A fortiori: *"if even the gods are not omniscient, certainly human beings are not"* [V].
5. From considerations of time (Iphicrates: you would have promised a statue before the deed; give it now).
6. Turning the opponent's words against him, which works only if he is more likely than you to have done the thing; it is ridiculous *"if you are attacking others for what you do or would do yourself, or are urging others to do what you neither do nor would do yourself"* [V].
7. Defining your terms (Iphicrates: *"Goodness is true nobility"* [V]).
8. The various senses of a word; and, unnumbered in the tape, logical division (*"All men do wrong from one of three motives, A, B, or C"* [V]).
10. Induction, including the Law of Theodectes: *"then men who have failed to secure other people's safety are not to be employed to secure our own"* [V].
11. Previous decisions, strongest if all or most people, the wise, the actual judges, or those they cannot gainsay have so decided.
12. Taking the parts of a subject separately.
13. From a thing's good and bad consequences (education brings unpopularity and wisdom).
14. Divarication, where each of two opposite courses has a good and a bad consequence (the priestess: say what is right and men hate you, say what is wrong and the gods do).
15. *"The things people approve of openly are not those which they approve of secretly"* [V]: openly they praise justice and nobility, in their hearts they prefer their advantage; establish the view your opponent has not adopted.
16. Rational correspondence (*"If you count tall boys men, you will next be voting short men boys"* [V]).
17. Same results, same antecedents.
18. Men reverse earlier choices.
19. Asserting that a possible motive is the real one.
20. Inducements and deterrents: we act if the action is *"possible, easy, and useful to ourselves or our friends or hurtful to our enemies"* [V]; the author says this topic forms the whole Art of Rhetoric of Pamphilus and of Callippus. [BT]
21. The incredible is likely true because people would not otherwise believe it.
22. Contradictions of dates, acts or words in the opponent's case.
23. For the slandered: explain the reason for the false impression.
24. Cause and effect present or absent together.
25. Whether the accused could have taken a better course; the author calls this fallacious: *"for it often becomes clear after the event how the action could have been done better, though before the event this was far from clear"* [V].
26. Examining an inconsistent contemplated and past action together (Xenophanes: do not mourn Leucothea if a goddess, do not sacrifice if a mortal).
27. Previous mistakes as grounds of accusation or defence (the Medea of Carcinus); the author says this formed the whole Art of Rhetoric before Theodorus. [BT]

A further line, set in quotation marks and unnumbered in the tape, draws meanings from names. The refutative enthymeme has the greater reputation *"because within a small space it works out two opposing arguments, and arguments put side by side are clearer to the audience"* [V]; the most applauded are those whose conclusions we foresee *"so long as they are not obvious at first sight-for part of the pleasure we feel is at our own intelligent anticipation"* [V] (Bk II, Part 23). [AR]

### Bk II, Part 24: spurious enthymemes

Besides genuine enthymemes there are those that look genuine but are not (Bk II, Part 24) [AR]:

1. From the words used: a compact antithetical utterance that passes for a conclusion (*"some he saved-others he avenged-the Greeks he freed"* [V]), or similar words for different things (the mouse as noble because of the "Mysteries").
2. Asserting of the whole what is true of the parts, or the reverse.
3. *"Another line is the use of indignant language, whether to support your own case or to overthrow your opponent's. We do this when we paint a highly-coloured picture of the situation without having proved the facts of it"* [V]: *"the hearer infers guilt or innocence, but no proof is given"* [V].
4. A Sign or single instance used as certain evidence (*"not every vicious man is a thief, though every thief is a vicious man"* [V]).
5. Representing the accidental as essential.
6. Argument from consequence (Paris lived alone on Ida, lofty people do this, so Paris was lofty), a fallacy by omission.
7. Representing as causes things that happened with or before the event: *"They assume that, because B happens after A, it happens because of A. Politicians are especially fond of taking this line."* [V] Demades blamed Demosthenes' policy because the war came after it.
8. Leaving out time and circumstances.
9. Confusing a particular probability with absolute probability. The author says Corax's Art of Rhetoric is composed of this line: a weakling accused of assault was not likely to do it, and a strong man was not likely to do it either, since he knew people would suspect him. [BT] *"This sort of argument illustrates what is meant by making the worse argument seem the better. Hence people were right in objecting to the training Protagoras undertook to give them. It was a fraud"* [V] (Bk II, Part 24).

### Bk II, Part 25: refutation

An argument is refuted by counter-syllogism or by objection. Counter-syllogisms come from the same lines, *"for the materials of syllogisms are the ordinary opinions of men, and such opinions often contradict each other"* [V]. Objections are raised in four ways: attacking the opponent's statement, putting forward a like statement, a contrary statement, or previous decisions (Bk II, Part 25). [AP]

Enthymemes rest on four kinds of alleged fact: *"(1) Probabilities, (2) Examples, (3) Infallible Signs, (4) Ordinary Signs"* [V]. Probabilities can always be met by an objection, but the refutation may be spurious, showing only that the premiss is *"not inevitably true"* [V] rather than not probable. Judges who accept this reason falsely: *"For they ought to decide by considering not merely what must be true but also what is likely to be true"* [V]. So the defendant's objection *"must state what is more usually true than the statement attacked"* [V], in frequency or exactness, best both (Bk II, Part 25). Fallible signs can be refuted even if the facts are correct. A negative instance refutes an argument from examples *"in so far as it is proved not inevitable"* [V]; where the positive examples are more numerous and more frequent, one contends that the present case *"is dissimilar, or that its conditions are dissimilar"* [V]. Infallible signs can be refuted only by showing the alleged fact does not exist (Bk II, Part 25). [AR]

### Bk II, Part 26: amplification; transition

Amplification and Depreciation are not an element (a line of argument) of enthymeme but one kind of enthymeme, used to show a thing great or small. Refutative enthymemes are not a different species from constructive ones, *"since the same means are employed by both parties"* [V]. *"An objection, on the other hand, is not an enthymeme at all"* [V] (Bk II, Part 26). Three points must be studied in making a speech: examples, maxims, enthymemes and *"in general the thought-element"* [V], then style, then arrangement (Bk II, Part 26). [AP]

## Theme 7: Style (Bk III, Parts 1–12)

### Bk III, Part 1: the three points; delivery

*"In making a speech one must study three points: first, the means of producing persuasion; second, the style, or language, to be used; third, the proper arrangement of the various parts of the speech."* [V] Persuasion has been shown to come *"(1) by working on the emotions of the judges themselves, (2) by giving them the right impression of the speakers' character, or (3) by proving the truth of the statements made"* [V] (Bk III, Part 1). *"For it is not enough to know what we ought to say; we must also say it as we ought"* [V]. [AR]

Delivery *"affects the success of a speech greatly; but hitherto the subject has been neglected"* [V]. It is *"a matter of the right management of the voice to express the various emotions"* [V]: *"These are the three things-volume of sound, modulation of pitch, and rhythm-that a speaker bears in mind."* [V] In drama the actors now count for more than the poets, *"so it is in the contests of public life, owing to the defects of our political institutions"* [V] (Bk III, Part 1). [AR]

The author qualifies the place of style and delivery: *"The right thing in speaking really is that we should be satisfied not to annoy our hearers, without trying to delight them: we ought in fairness to fight our case with no help beyond the bare facts"* [V], but other things matter *"owing to the defects of our hearers"* [V]. The way a thing is said affects its intelligibility, *"Not, however, so much importance as people think. All such arts are fanciful and meant to charm the hearer. Nobody uses fine language when teaching geometry."* [V] (Bk III, Part 1) Prose language is distinct from poetry's; Gorgias's poetical colour came from poets winning fame through fine language, and *"Even now most uneducated people think that poetical language makes the finest discourses. That is not true"* [V] (Bk III, Part 1). [AR]

### Bk III, Part 2: clearness, appropriateness, metaphor

*"Style to be good must be clear, as is proved by the fact that speech which fails to convey a plain meaning will fail to do just what speech has to do. It must also be appropriate, avoiding both meanness and undue elevation"* [V]. Clearness comes from current and ordinary words; some unfamiliarity gives distinction, *"people like what strikes them, and are struck by what is out of the way"* [V], but less in prose than verse (Bk III, Part 2). [AR]

*"We can now see that a writer must disguise his art and give the impression of speaking naturally and not artificially. Naturalness is persuasive, artificiality is the contrary; for our hearers are prejudiced and think we have some design against them, as if we were mixing their wines for them."* [V] (Bk III, Part 2) The art is hidden by taking single words from ordinary speech. *"Words of ambiguous meaning are chiefly useful to enable the sophist to mislead his hearers."* [V] [AR]

Metaphor gives *"clearness, charm, and distinction as nothing else can: and it is not a thing whose use can be taught by one man to another"* [V]. It must be fitting; to compliment, draw it from something better in the same line, to disparage, from something worse: *"We can thus call a crime a mistake, or a mistake a crime. We can say that a thief 'took' a thing, or that he 'plundered' his victim."* [V] Metaphors for nameless things should come from kindred things; good riddles furnish good metaphors (Bk III, Part 2). Against the sophist Bryson, who held there is no foul language because the meaning is the same whatever the words: *"This is untrue. One term may describe a thing more truly than another, may be more like it, and set it more intimately before our eyes."* [V] Orestes may be a "mother-slayer" or his "father's avenger" (Bk III, Part 2). [AR]

### Bk III, Part 3: bad taste

Bad taste takes four forms: misused compound words, strange words, long, unseasonable or frequent epithets, and inappropriate metaphor (Bk III, Part 3). Of Alcidamas's epithets: *"he does not use them as the seasoning of the meat, but as the meat itself"* [V]; *"for when the sense is plain, you only obscure and spoil its clearness by piling up words"* [V]. Metaphors fail when ridiculous, too grand and theatrical, or far-fetched and obscure; Alcidamas's examples *"fail, for the reasons given, to carry the hearer with them"* [V] (Bk III, Part 3). [AP]

### Bk III, Part 4: the simile

*"The Simile also is a metaphor; the difference is but slight."* [V] "He leapt on the foe as a lion" is a simile; "the lion leapt" a metaphor. Similes are useful in prose but not often, *"since they are of the nature of poetry"* [V] (Bk III, Part 4). The author gives examples from Androtion, Plato's Republic, Pericles and Demosthenes, and adds that a proportional metaphor must apply reciprocally: if a drinking-bowl is the shield of Dionysus, a shield may be called the drinking-bowl of Ares (Bk III, Part 4). [AE]

### Bk III, Part 5: correctness

*"The foundation of good style is correctness of language, which falls under five heads"* [V]: the right use of connecting words; *"calling things by their own special names and not by vague general ones"* [V]; avoiding ambiguity; correct gender (Protagoras's classification of nouns); and correct number (Bk III, Part 5). On ambiguity: *"Diviners use these vague generalities about the matter in hand because their predictions are thus, as a rule, less likely to be falsified."* [V] The oracle-monger is more likely right *"if he simply says that a thing will happen than if he says when it will happen"* [V] (Bk III, Part 5). [AR]

*"It is a general rule that a written composition should be easy to read and therefore easy to deliver."* [V] Heracleitus is hard to punctuate. Obscurity also arises when details are inserted before the meaning is made clear: say "I meant to set out after telling him; then this, that, and the other thing occurred" rather than the reverse (Bk III, Part 5). [AP]

### Bk III, Part 6: impressiveness and conciseness

For impressiveness: describe a thing instead of naming it (for conciseness, name it); use metaphor and epithet without poetical effect; plural for singular; an article with each word; plenty of connecting words (for conciseness, fewer); and Antimachus's method of describing a thing by attributes it lacks (Bk III, Part 6). [AP]

### Bk III, Part 7: appropriateness

*"Your language will be appropriate if it expresses emotion and character, and if it corresponds to its subject."* [V] Correspondence means not speaking *"casually about weighty matters, nor solemnly about trivial ones"* [V] (Bk III, Part 7).
