Aptness of language makes people believe a story: *"their minds draw the false conclusion that you are to be trusted from the fact that others behave as you do when things are as you describe them"* [V]. *"Besides, an emotional speaker always makes his audience feel with him, even when there is nothing in his arguments; which is why many speakers try to overwhelm their audience by mere noise."* [V] (Bk III, Part 7) [AR]

Language also displays character by class (age, sex, nationality) and disposition: *"a rustic and an educated man will not say the same things nor speak in the same way"* [V]. The device "Who does not know this?", used *"to nauseous excess"* [V], shames the hearer into agreeing. *"The best way to counteract any exaggeration is the well-worn device by which the speaker puts in some criticism of himself"* [V]; and not everything should correspond, so harsh words should not come with a harsh voice and face, or *"the artificial character of each detail becomes apparent"* [V] (Bk III, Part 7). [AR]

### Bk III, Part 8: prose rhythm

*"The form of a prose composition should be neither metrical nor destitute of rhythm. The metrical form destroys the hearer's trust by its artificial appearance"* [V], while unrhythmical language is *"too unlimited"* [V]. The heroic rhythm has dignity but lacks spoken tones; the iambic is ordinary speech; the trochee is akin to wild dancing; the paean is to be adopted because no definite metre arises from it. A sentence should end on the long syllable, so that its close is marked *"not by the scribe, or by his period-mark in the margin, but by the rhythm itself"* [V] (Bk III, Part 8). [AP]

### Bk III, Part 9: free-running and periodic style

The free-running style *"has no natural stopping-places"* [V] and is unsatisfying, *"one always likes to sight a stopping-place in front of one"* [V], as runners collapse only at the goal (Bk III, Part 9). *"By a period I mean a portion of speech that has in itself a beginning and an end, being at the same time not too big to be taken in at a glance."* [V] Periodic language is satisfying because it is the reverse of indefinite and the hearer feels he is grasping something and has reached a definite conclusion; it is easy to follow *"because it can easily be remembered"* [V], since periodic language can be numbered. Members should be neither curt nor long: one too short often makes the listener stumble, too long leaves him behind (Bk III, Part 9). [AR]

Antithesis sets opposites in the two members. It satisfies *"because the significance of contrasted ideas is easily felt, especially when they are thus put side by side, and also because it has the effect of a logical argument; it is by putting two opposing conclusions side by side that you prove one of them false"* [V] (Bk III, Part 9). Parisosis and paromoeosis are also defined. [AR]

### Bk III, Part 10: lively sayings

Their invention *"can only come through natural talent or long practice"* [V]. *"We will begin by remarking that we all naturally find it agreeable to get hold of new ideas easily"* [V]. *"Now strange words simply puzzle us; ordinary words convey only what we know already; it is from metaphor that we can best get hold of something fresh."* [V] (Bk III, Part 10) People are not much taken either by obvious arguments or by those that puzzle, but by those *"which convey their information to us as soon as we hear them, provided we had not the information already; or which the mind only just fails to keep up with"* [V]. The words should *"set the scene before our eyes; for events ought to be seen in progress rather than in prospect. So we must aim at these three points: Antithesis, Metaphor, and Actuality."* [V] (Bk III, Part 10) The proportional metaphor is the most taking kind, as in Pericles's saying that the loss of the young men in war was *"as if the spring were taken out of the year"* [V] (Bk III, Part 10). [AR]

### Bk III, Part 11: making them see things; surprise

*"By 'making them see things' I mean using expressions that represent things as in a state of activity."* [V] Homer gives metaphorical life to lifeless things (Bk III, Part 11). Metaphors should come from things related but not obviously so, as *"an acute mind will perceive resemblances even in things far apart"* [V]: Archytas said an arbitrator and an altar were the same, *"since the injured fly to both for refuge"* [V] (Bk III, Part 11). [AR]

Liveliness also comes from surprise: *"His mind seems to say, 'Yes, to be sure; I never thought of that'."* [V] Such sayings must fit the facts, and *"the more briefly and antithetically such sayings can be expressed, the more taking they are, for antithesis impresses the new idea more firmly and brevity more quickly"* [V]. They need *"either some personal application or some merit of expression, if they are to be true without being commonplace"* [V] (Bk III, Part 11). Successful similes are *"in a sense metaphors"* [V]; proverbs and successful hyperboles are metaphors too; *"Hyperboles are for young men to use"* [V] and do not suit an elderly speaker (Bk III, Part 11). [AP]

### Bk III, Part 12: the style proper to each kind

*"It should be observed that each kind of rhetoric has its own appropriate style. The style of written prose is not that of spoken oratory, nor are those of political and forensic speaking the same."* [V] The written style is more finished; the spoken admits dramatic delivery. Repetition and strings of unconnected words are condemned in writing but work spoken, and must be acted; omitting conjunctions *"makes a single one into many"* [V] (Bk III, Part 12). [AR]

*"Now the style of oratory addressed to public assemblies is really just like scene-painting. The bigger the throng, the more distant is the point of view: so that, in the one and the other, high finish in detail is superfluous and seems better away."* [V] Forensic style is more finished, and more so before a single judge, *"with whom there is very little room for rhetorical artifices, since he can take the whole thing in better, and judge of what is to the point and what is not"* [V]. Ceremonial oratory is the most literary (Bk III, Part 12). [AR] To call style "agreeable" or "magnificent" adds nothing; prolix style is not clear, nor curt: *"Plainly the middle way suits best."* [V] (Bk III, Part 12) [AP]

## Theme 8: Arrangement (Bk III, Parts 13–19)

### Bk III, Part 13: the necessary parts of a speech

*"A speech has two parts. You must state your case, and you must prove it."* [V] Proof must be proof of something, and the only use of a statement is the proof that follows. *"The current division is absurd"* [V]: narration belongs only to forensic speeches; introduction, comparison of arguments and recapitulation appear in political speeches only when two policies contend; short speeches need no epilogue. The essential parts are Statement and Argument; a speech *"cannot in any case have more than Introduction, Statement, Argument, and Epilogue"* [V] (Bk III, Part 13). Refutation and comparison are part of the arguments. Against Theodorus's subdivisions and Licymnius's invented names: *"we ought only to bring in a new name if it indicates a real species with distinct specific qualities; otherwise the practice is pointless and silly"* [V] (Bk III, Part 13). [AR]

### Bk III, Part 14: the introduction

In speeches of display, the introduction may begin with whatever best takes the speaker's fancy (praise, censure, advice, appeals to the audience) and then lead into the theme. In forensic speeches, as in prologues and epic, *"a foretaste of the theme is given, intended to inform the hearers of it in advance instead of keeping their minds in suspense. Anything vague puzzles them: so give them a grasp of the beginning, and they can hold fast to it and follow the argument."* [V] *"This, then, is the most essential function and distinctive property of the introduction, to show what the aim of the speech is; and therefore no introduction ought to be employed where the subject is not long or intricate."* [V] (Bk III, Part 14) [AR]

Other introductions are remedial, concerned with the speaker, hearer, subject or opponent. The defendant removes prejudice at the start, *"must clear away any obstacles"* [V]; the prosecutor excites prejudice at the close, *"so that the judges may more easily remember"* [V] (Bk III, Part 14). Appeals to the hearer seek goodwill, resentment, attention or distraction. Hearers attend to what touches themselves and what is important, surprising or agreeable. This all concerns *"the weak-minded tendency of the hearer to listen to what is beside the point"* [V]; where it is absent, a summary statement of the subject suffices. Calls for attention belong anywhere but the beginning, *"when every one is listening with most attention"* [V]. *"It is plain that such introductions are addressed not to ideal hearers, but to hearers as we find them."* [V] *"Introductions are popular with those whose case is weak, or looks weak; it pays them to dwell on anything rather than the actual facts of it."* [V] (Bk III, Part 14) The two things to aim at are goodwill and compassion. Political introductions are rare, since the subject is known. [AR]

### Bk III, Part 15: dealing with prejudice

Ways to dispel prejudice: meet the issue directly by denying the fact, or the harm, or its extent, or the injustice, or the disgrace. *"Thus Iphicrates replying to Nausicrates, admitted that he had done the deed alleged, and that he had done Nausicrates harm, but not that he had done him wrong."* [V] Admit the wrong but balance it with other facts. *"Another way is to allege that your action was due to mistake, or bad luck, or necessity"* [V]. Balance motive against deed: the damage was accidental, *"'I should indeed be a detestable person if I had deliberately intended this result.'"* [V] (Bk III, Part 15) [AP]

Further: the accuser is subject to the same suspicion; others so suspected were innocent; the question is already decided; or denounce calumny itself, showing *"that it raises false issues, and that it means a lack of confidence in the merits of his case"* [V]. The calumniator's method, *"of thoroughly skilful and unscrupulous prosecutors"* [V], is to praise a trifling merit at length and attack an important failing briefly. Since an action can be done from many motives, the calumniator picks the worse and the apologist the better (Bk III, Part 15). [AR]

### Bk III, Part 16: narration

In ceremonial oratory, narration is intermittent rather than continuous, because a continuous narrative *"is hard to keep in mind"* [V]; well-known deeds usually need no narration, and the speaker has only to apply them (Bk III, Part 16). *"Nowadays it is said, absurdly enough, that the narration should be rapid."* [V] As the baker was asked, "What, can't you make it right?": *"Here, again, rightness does not consist either in rapidity or in conciseness, but in the happy mean; that is, in saying just so much as will make the facts plain"* [V] (Bk III, Part 16). The defendant makes less of narration and should not waste time on admitted fact unless it bears on his own contention; events should be spoken of as past *"except where they excite pity or indignation by being represented as present"* [V]. [AR]

*"The narration should depict character"* [V], for example, by *"the indication of moral purpose"* [V]; mathematical discourses depict no character because they represent nobody pursuing an end. Let words seem inspired by moral purpose rather than intelligence: *"For the other way shows good sense, but this shows good character"* [V]. Where a detail seems incredible, add its cause (Bk III, Part 16). Use the emotions' familiar manifestations, *"he went away scowling at me"* [V]: *"These details carry conviction: the audience take the truth of what they know as so much evidence for the truth of what they do not."* [V] Bring yourself on stage in the right character from the first, *"but do not let them see what you are about"* [V] (Bk III, Part 16). [AR]

*"In political oratory there is very little opening for narration; nobody can 'narrate' what has not yet happened. If there is narration at all, it will be of past events, the recollection of which is to help the hearers to make better plans for the future."* [V] A hard-to-believe statement needs a guarantee, an explanation and particulars (Bk III, Part 16). [AR]

### Bk III, Part 17: the arguments

The arguments must bear on the question in dispute, which falls under four heads: the act was not committed; it did no harm; it was less than alleged; it was justified. *"It should be noted that only where the question in dispute falls under the first of these heads can it be true that one of the two parties is necessarily a rogue. Here ignorance cannot be pleaded, as it might if the dispute were whether the act was justified or not."* [V] (Bk III, Part 17) [AR]

In ceremonial speeches the case is developed mainly by showing deeds noble and useful; the facts are taken on trust, and proof is offered only on the rare occasions when they are not easily credible or have been attributed to someone else. In political speeches one may maintain a proposal is impracticable, unjust, useless or less important than claimed; *"Note any falsehoods about irrelevant matters-they will look like proof that his other statements also are false."* [V] Example suits political oratory, enthymeme forensic, because *"there is no contingency in what has now already happened"* [V] (Bk III, Part 17). [AR]

Do not use a continuous succession of enthymemes; do not make enthymemes on every point; *"And avoid the enthymeme form when you are trying to rouse feeling; for it will either kill the feeling or will itself fall flat"* [V]; nor where depicting character, since *"the process of demonstration can express neither moral character nor moral purpose"* [V]. Maxims, which do express character, belong in the arguments and the narration (Bk III, Part 17). [AR]

*"Political oratory is a more difficult task than forensic; and naturally so, since it deals with the future, whereas the pleader deals with the past"* [V]; forensic oratory has a basis in law, while political oratory affords fewer chances than any other kind for leisurely digressions, unless the speaker's set purpose is to divert the hearers' attention. If you have no enthymemes, fall back on moral discourse: *"after all, it is more fitting for a good man to display himself as an honest fellow than as a subtle reasoner"* [V] (Bk III, Part 17). [AR]

The reply to the opponent is part of the arguments. The first speaker puts his own arguments first and then refutes the other side's in advance, unless the other side has many arguments. The later speaker must first answer the opponent, especially if well received: *"You should, therefore, make room in the minds of the audience for your coming speech; and this will be done by getting your opponent's speech out of the way."* [V] (Bk III, Part 17) Assertions that would seem tedious or abusive in one's own mouth go into the mouth of a third person; enthymemes can be restated as maxims (Bk III, Part 17). [AP]

### Bk III, Part 18: interrogation and jests

Interrogation suits four moments: when one more question lands the opponent in absurdity (Pericles and Lampon); when one premiss is obvious and the opponent must grant the other (Socrates and Meletus); when it shows him contradicting himself or common belief; and when he can answer only evasively. *"In other cases do not attempt interrogation; for if your opponent gets in an objection, you are felt to have been worsted. You cannot ask a series of questions owing to the incapacity of the audience to follow them"* [V] (Bk III, Part 18). [AR]

In replying, *"you must meet ambiguous questions by drawing reasonable distinctions, not by a curt answer"* [V]. For questions that seem to involve a contradiction, offer the explanation at the outset of the answer, before the opponent asks the next question or draws his conclusion. When the conclusion is put as a question, justify the answer: Sophocles, asked whether he had voted for the Four Hundred and thought it wicked, answered yes to both, *"for there was nothing better to do"* [V]; the ephor said the others were justly executed because *"they were bribed to do it, and I did it from conviction"* [V] (Bk III, Part 18). [AE]

On jests the author endorses Gorgias: *"Gorgias said that you should kill your opponents' earnestness with jesting and their jesting with earnestness; in which he was right."* [V] [BT] *"Irony better befits a gentleman than buffoonery; the ironical man jokes to amuse himself, the buffoon to amuse other people."* [V] (Bk III, Part 18) [AR]

### Bk III, Part 19: the epilogue

*"The Epilogue has four parts. You must (1) make the audience well-disposed towards yourself and ill-disposed towards your opponent (2) magnify or minimize the leading facts, (3) excite the required state of emotion in your hearers, and (4) refresh their memories."* [V] (Bk III, Part 19) The facts must be admitted before their importance is discussed, *"just as the body cannot grow except from something already present"* [V]. The emotions to excite are *"pity, indignation, anger, hatred, envy, emulation, pugnacity"* [V] (Bk III, Part 19). [AR]

Repetition belongs in the epilogue, not the introduction, where *"some wrongly recommend"* [V] it: the introduction states the subject so the point to be judged is plain, the epilogue summarises the arguments. *"The first step in this reviewing process is to observe that you have done what you undertook to do. You must, then, state what you have said and why you have said it."* [V] Compare your case with the opponent's point by point or follow the order of the arguments (Bk III, Part 19). The conclusion suits the disconnected style: *"I have done. You have heard me. The facts are before you. I ask for your judgement."* [V] (Bk III, Part 19) [AE]

## Key statistics (with provenance)

The source is a treatise, not an empirical study; it reports no measurements. Its load-bearing figures are its own enumerations.

| Metric | Value | Classification |
|---|---|---|
| Modes of persuasion furnished by the spoken word | three (speaker's character; hearers' frame of mind; proof or apparent proof) | "there are three kinds" [V] (Bk I, Part 2) |
| Divisions of oratory | three (political, forensic, ceremonial) | "three divisions" [V] (Bk I, Part 3) |
| Main subjects of political deliberation | five (ways and means, war and peace, national defence, imports and exports, legislation) | "some five in number" [V] (Bk I, Part 4) |
| Forms of government | four (democracy, oligarchy, aristocracy, monarchy) | "The forms of government are four" [V] (Bk I, Part 8) |
| Causes of action | seven (chance, nature, compulsion, habit, reasoning, anger, appetite) | "seven causes" [V] (Bk I, Part 10) |
| Non-technical means of persuasion | five (laws, witnesses, contracts, tortures, oaths) | "five in number" [V] (Bk I, Part 15) |
| Sources of confidence in the speaker | three (good sense, good moral character, goodwill) | "There are three things" [V] (Bk II, Part 1) |
| Kinds of slighting | three (contempt, spite, insolence) | "three kinds of slighting" [V] (Bk II, Part 2) |
| Prime of life | body 30–35; mind about 49 | "from thirty to five-and-thirty; the mind about forty-nine" [V] (Bk II, Part 14) |
| Lines of argument for enthymemes | numbered 1–27 with no 9; logical division (after 8) and meanings from names unnumbered | [AP] (Bk II, Part 23) |
| Kinds of alleged fact for enthymemes | four (probabilities, examples, infallible signs, ordinary signs) | "four kinds of alleged fact" [V] (Bk II, Part 25) |
| Forms of bad taste | four | "any of four forms" [V] (Bk III, Part 3) |
| Heads of correctness | five | "five heads" [V] (Bk III, Part 5) |
| Necessary parts of a speech | two (statement, argument); at most four (introduction, statement, argument, epilogue) | [AP] (Bk III, Part 13) |
| Parts of the epilogue | four | "four parts" [V] (Bk III, Part 19) |

## Connections the author makes in the text

- Works cited in the text as fuller treatments: the *Topics* (handling a popular audience; induction and syllogism; objections; senses of "rightly"), the *Analytics* (syllogism and necessary premisses; signs), the *Methodics*, the *Politics* (forms of government), and the treatise on the *Art of Poetry* / *Poetics* (the ludicrous; kinds of words and metaphor; jests); also the *Theodectea* on the beginnings of periods (Bk I, Parts 1, 2, 8, 11; Bk II, Parts 22, 23, 25, 26; Bk III, Parts 1, 2, 9, 18). [AP]
- The writers of current treatises on rhetoric, unnamed, criticised for treating non-essentials and neglecting political oratory (Bk I, Part 1). [BT]
- Corax, whose Art of Rhetoric the author says is composed of the spurious particular-probability line; Protagoras, whose training people were "right in objecting to"; Protagoras is also credited, neutrally, with classifying nouns as male, female and inanimate (Bk II, Part 24; Bk III, Part 5). [BT]
- Callippus, whose Art of Rhetoric the author says is made up of the consequences line with the addition of Possibility and the other lines of that kind; Pamphilus and Callippus, whose Arts he says consist wholly of the topic of inducements and deterrents; Theodorus, whose followers' subdivisions of narration he calls pointless, whose "novelties" he cites approvingly, and before whom the previous-mistakes line made up the whole Art of Rhetoric; Licymnius, whose invented names he mocks and whose remark on the beauty of words he cites (Bk II, Part 23; Bk III, Parts 2, 11, 13). [BT]
- Thrasymachus ("Appeals to Pity"; the paean); Glaucon of Teos (delivery in poetry); Prodicus (calls for attention) (Bk III, Parts 1, 8, 14). [BT]
- Gorgias: criticised for poetical language and over-poetic metaphors, approved on jests (Bk III, Parts 1, 3, 18). Isocrates: cited often, including for comparison in praise *"owing to his want of familiarity with forensic pleading"* [V] (Bk I, Part 9) and for attacks within political speeches (Bk III, Part 17). Alcidamas: criticised for tasteless epithets and metaphors (Bk III, Part 3). [BT]
- Socrates: his illustrative parallel on choosing by lot, his saying about praising Athenians to Athenians, and his questioning of Meletus (Bk I, Part 9; Bk II, Part 20; Bk III, Part 18). [BT]
- Poets and orators throughout as illustrations, chiefly Homer, Sophocles, Euripides, Simonides, Pericles, Iphicrates and Demosthenes. [AE]

## Positions the author explicitly frames against

- *The current treatises on rhetoric.* They say nothing about enthymemes, deal with non-essentials such as arousing prejudice, pity and anger, and write about pleading in court while ignoring political oratory (Bk I, Part 1).
- *That the speaker's personal goodness contributes nothing to persuasion,* which the author says some writers assume; he answers that character may almost be called the most effective means of persuasion the speaker possesses (Bk I, Part 2).
- *Treating rhetoric and dialectic as sciences of definite subjects* rather than practical faculties, which he says destroys their nature (Bk I, Part 4).
- *Particular probability passed off as absolute probability* (Corax's Art; Protagoras's training), *"making the worse argument seem the better"* [V] (Bk II, Part 24).
- *That poetical language makes the finest discourses,* a view he attributes to most uneducated people (Bk III, Part 1).
- *Bryson's claim that there is no foul language* (Bk III, Part 2).
- *That style should be called "agreeable" or "magnificent"* as further qualities (Bk III, Part 12).
- *The current division of the parts of a speech,* and the multiplication of names by Theodorus's followers and Licymnius (Bk III, Part 13).
- *Calls for attention placed at the beginning of a speech,* which he calls ridiculous (Bk III, Part 14).
- *That narration should be rapid* (Bk III, Part 16).
- *Repeating one's points in the introduction,* which *"some wrongly recommend"* [V] (Bk III, Part 19).

## Citation and source-integrity notes

**Conversion and coverage.** Conversion of the Internet Classics Archive's plain-text file added Markdown heading marks (`# Book N`, `## Part N`), changed `BOOK` to `Book`, trimmed heading whitespace and removed 63 blank lines around headings. All non-heading text matches the original word for word. The tape has 6,502 lines and 68,240 words; the original has 6,565 lines and 68,177 words. Both contain 60 numbered parts. Every line, 1–6502, was read in sequence. Image scope: text-only; the source has no images.

**What [V] means here.** The tape is an English translation. Every [V] marks W. Rhys Roberts's English exactly as the tape prints it; none of Aristotle's Greek survives on the tape apart from scattered, garbled transliterations, and none is quoted. Claims in this reference are claims about what the Roberts translation says.

**Citation style.** `(Bk N, Part M)`, because the tape carries no Bekker numbers or page anchors. "Part" numbers are the archive's divisions as headed in the tape.

**Text as printed.** Quotations keep the tape's spelling and punctuation, including hyphens standing for dashes ("pity-one might") and the spacing "'possibly'or". The tape also has slips, among them "hetter" (Bk I, Part 7), "mysell" (Bk I, Part 7), "as ahas" (Bk I, Part 15), "As in the therefore" (Bk I, Part 2), "alway" (Bk II, Part 20) and "snot" (Bk III, Part 16). Several passages are printed in square brackets without explanation ("[or by the worthless]", Bk I, Part 6; "[its opposite is meanness of spirit]", Bk I, Part 9; "[our lovers,]", Bk I, Part 11; the closing sentences on torture and on the non-technical modes, Bk I, Part 15); they are reported as printed. Three sentences break off with ellipses (the Alcidamas citation, Bk I, Part 13; "As for the defence,...", Bk II, Part 23; the narration of Critias's deeds, Bk III, Part 16). In Bk II, Part 23 the numbering skips 9 (logical division follows line 8 unnumbered), and a final line on meanings from names is set inside quotation marks with no number. Verse quotations are hard-wrapped in the tape with stray quotation marks at line ends; two short ones are quoted without those marks ("Potter to potter and builder to builder begrudge their reward", Bk II, Part 4; "Potter against potter", Bk II, Part 10).

**Provenance and licence.** Publication details (Clarendon Press, 1924; Works of Aristotle vol. XI), the public-domain licence, the fetch date, URL and checksum come from the operator's metadata; the tape itself names only the translator and the archive. The archive's closing "Copyright statement" claims copyright in its World Wide Web presentation ("All rights reserved under international and pan-American copyright conventions"); it is the archive's, not part of the work. The licence and scope decision is the operator's.
